title: GainCtrl: Predicting Remaining Gains for Efficient LLM Agent Execution
shortTitle: GainCtrl: Predicting Remaining Gains for Efficient LLM Agent Execution
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are widely used to power agents that interact with tools and environments to solve complex tasks. Repeated attempts improve the quality of tool-using agents, but continued execution incurs additional costs even when it is unlikely to improve the best result ultimately returned. This raises the question of when to stop an attempt to reduce execution cost while preserving task-level Best-of-N quality. To address this question, we introduce GainCtrl, a gain-based execution controller for LLMs. In GainCtrl, a lightweight CPU predictor uses interaction histories to estimate expected positive gains over retained scores, which are then used to guide stopping decisions with calibrated thresholds to limit the loss in mean Best-of-N task quality. We evaluate the controller through trajectory replay across three environments and three LLM actors. Comparisons of interpolated quality-cost Pareto frontiers show that GainCtrl generally uses fewer tokens than baselines at matched target quality. Fixed policies also achieve quality close to that of full execution while substantially reducing token consumption. The predictor runs at millisecond latency on a single CPU thread, supporting repeated monitoring without access to LLM internals.

title: CLIFT: Contrastive LiDAR Instance Features for 3D Pedestrian Tracking
shortTitle: CLIFT: Contrastive LiDAR Instance Features for 3D Pedestrian Tracking
abstract: A social robot has to keep track of the people around it over time to plan its motion, a task handled by 3D multi-object tracking. For the LiDAR modality, trackers usually sit on top of a detector and link its detections across frames with a separate motion model or re-identification network. We instead show how a 3D LiDAR detector itself can be turned into a tracker by adding an instance-level contrastive objective on its intermediate voxel features. Each embedding is read from the voxels inside a detected box, and boxes are matched across frames by cosine similarity and the Hungarian algorithm, without a motion model. The detector backbone is fine-tuned together with this objective, which learns identity-aware features while leaving detection accuracy essen- tially intact. Because the method uses only the voxel features that Li- DAR detectors already produce, it is backbone-agnostic. On the JRDB 3D tracking leaderboard our LiDAR-only tracker ranks first on HOTA (38.58) and IDF1 (37.99), 13.04 and 9.30 points above the next pub- lished method, and second on MOTA and OSPA. Code is available at https://hermak56.github.io/CLIFT/.

title: Robotic Reward Models in the Foundation-Model Era
shortTitle: Robotic Reward Models in the Foundation-Model Era
abstract: Robotic reward models (RRMs) use foundation models to replace per-task reward engineering with reusable, task-conditioned evaluation. Yet under one name, their outputs answer different questions, from whether a task succeeded to which execution is better. This survey organizes 114 methods into five semantic families by the question their native outputs answer: Outcome, Absolute Progress, Relative, Temporal Value, and Hybrid. Within this taxonomy, we review how model design determines what an evaluator can judge, how raw experience becomes supervision, and how existing evaluation practice tests the result. The review exposes a gap: agreement with demonstration order and downstream policy gains do not show whether a reward tracks task fulfillment. We therefore introduce RRM-Bench-1K, 1,117 real-robot videos of closed-loop executions with task-state and camera-evidence labels, and four contrast suites that separate the credited condition from its usual cues. A unified study of 27 evaluators shows that the strongest final scores rank whole executions well enough for selection and filtering. Dense credit, however, follows the progression of an execution more closely than its task state, and no evaluator signals when the decisive view is missing. How much fidelity a reward model needs therefore depends on the decision it drives. We outline directions from real-failure supervision to metrics that separate task state from chronology, and open-source RRM-Hub, a toolbox in which 14 existing RRMs can be readily applied and new evaluators tested on the same capabilities.

title: A Seismic Foundation Model for Dense Feature Extraction
shortTitle: A Seismic Foundation Model for Dense Feature Extraction
abstract: Deep-learning-based seismic interpretation is constrained by scarce high-quality annotations, and most existing models are trained separately for individual tasks. We present SeisDFE, a 7B-parameter seismic foundation model for dense feature extraction, pretrained on 5.34 million 2D images derived from more than 500 seismic volumes. A three-stage pretraining strategy, combining discriminative self-supervised learning, Gram feature anchoring, and multi-resolution adaptation, improves feature discriminability while preserving spatial coherence. With its encoder frozen, SeisDFE supports seismic facies classification, salt detection, fault detection, and relative geologic time estimation. It outperforms existing seismic foundation models on all four tasks and a natural-image-pretrained model on all but fault detection, with the largest gains under scarce supervision: using only two annotated sections of the F3 dataset, it improves whole-volume mIoU by 12-19 percentage points over the baselines. The learned features remain effective with task-specific decoders and extend to synthetic-to-field transfer and sparse 3D geobody interpretation. These results show that large-scale seismic pretraining organizes geological information into dense representations that are directly reusable across interpretation tasks.

title: GPRM: Global Perspective Process Reward Model
shortTitle: GPRM: Global Perspective Process Reward Model
abstract: Process Reward Models (PRMs) are widely used for step-level evaluation of multi-step reasoning in large language models, but existing methods are often limited by weak historical dependency modeling and insufficient global awareness. They typically fail to leverage prior step evaluations for coherent judgment and lack visibility into subsequent reasoning, leading to suboptimal assessment of intermediate steps. To address this issue, we propose the Global Perspective Process Reward Model (GPRM), which jointly models the problem, previous reasoning steps and their evaluations, the current step, and future steps to enable history-aware and globally informed process evaluation. We further introduce a structured evaluation framework along four dimensions---look back, look ahead, self-check, and goal alignment---to assess prior consistency, future plausibility, step validity, and task alignment. Based on this framework, we construct datasets for supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (GRPO). Experiments show that, despite using less training data and smaller model sizes, GPRM outperforms strong baseline models by 7.8 and 5.4 points on PRMBench and ProcessBench, respectively. GPRM also generalizes well across tasks, surpassing the GPT-4.1 baseline on Agent Error Bench, improving strong baselines by around 4 points under test-time scaling (TTS), and achieving competitive performance on PPE.

title: Instant Weight-Space Consolidation for Long-Term Memory in LLMs
shortTitle: Instant Weight-Space Consolidation for Long-Term Memory in LLMs
abstract: Agentic memory systems give LLMs persistent memory by extracting experience into text and retrieving it at query time, but the model itself does not evolve: however many interactions it has had, it starts each query the same. Extraction errors compound, implicit cross-session patterns that no single fragment states cannot be surfaced, and the construction cost grows with every conversation. Fine-tuning on past interactions does change the weights, but requires backpropagation at serving time and degrades on long histories. We introduce CLAM (Carried Latent Adapter Memory), which combines the strengths of both: a recurrent hypernetwork performs parametric consolidation, compiling a stream of session activations into a low-rank adapter in a single forward pass with no gradient steps and no language-model generation calls, while a complementary episodic buffer supplies verbatim detail at inference. A gated latent state carries knowledge across sessions in fixed size, so the parametric memory accumulates without growing. On LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S across three open models (2-7B parameters), CLAM leads all agentic baselines by 1-45 points and all gradient-based parametric methods by 10-45 points, while requiring zero generative LLM calls, zero gradient steps, and 3-151x less wall-clock time than extraction systems to build its memory. The two channels are complementary: the consolidated adapter adds 12-15 accuracy points when the episodic buffer misses the gold evidence, and still adds 4-5 points even with an oracle buffer.

title: STA: A Split Temporal Adversary Method for Evaluating Robustness of Multimodal RL-based Driving Policies
shortTitle: STA: A Split Temporal Adversary Method for Evaluating Robustness of Multimodal RL-based Driving Policies
abstract: Multimodal reinforcement learning (MRL) offers a promising paradigm for autonomous driving by jointly leveraging complementary sensor observations to learn effective decision-making policies. However, its effectiveness critically depends on temporal alignment across modalities, making temporal inconsistency a fundamental vulnerability. Even subtle misalignment or latency can corrupt fused representations and ultimately lead to decision failures. Existing studies have explored adversarial attacks to induce cross-modal temporal inconsistencies, thereby enabling systematic evaluation of the temporal robustness of MRL policies. However, existing methods remain limited in generality, realism, and adaptivity. To address these limitations, we propose the Split Temporal Adversary (STA), which formulates multimodal temporal attacks as a unified decision process that jointly optimizes attack timing and modality selection under realistic policy-aware and budget-constrained settings. STA includes two mechanisms: a) a unified multimodal temporal perturbation mechanism that delays observations via historical states, removing the need for modality-specific noise; b) a split multimodal adversarial decision mechanism that jointly optimizes attack timing and modality selection through adaptive optimization while leveraging the victim policy's clean actions to identify sensitive decision patterns. We provide a theoretical analysis of the induced distribution shift and a modality selection principle. Experiments in the CARLA simulator show that STA more than doubles the collision rate of the strongest baseline against PPO while using 17.8\% fewer attack attempts, and that it generalizes to a VLM-based driving policy. These results reveal temporal consistency as a critical vulnerability, highlighting temporal robustness as essential for safe autonomous driving.

title: UNITE: Consolidating Embodied VLM Specialists via Shared-Anchor One-Bit Factorization
shortTitle: UNITE: Consolidating Embodied VLM Specialists via Shared-Anchor One-Bit Factorization
abstract: Embodied capabilities such as visual grounding, spatial reasoning, navigation, and driving understanding are often developed in separate vision-language specialists fine-tuned from a common pretrained model.Deploying the specialists separately multiplies storage, whereas merging them into one dense model forces conflicting task updates to share parameters and loses part of each specialist's expertise.We introduce UNITE, a framework that consolidates such specialists into a compact shared-backbone mixture of experts. UNITE keeps the feed-forward block of each specialist as a routable expert and represents the expert bank through a shared-anchor one-bit factorization: a shared floating-point anchor plus expert-specific, row-scaled binary deviations.The anchor is optimized jointly with the scales and signs through closed-form alternating updates, using only source weights and no calibration data.Router adaptation then adjusts token-level expert selection with the backbone and experts frozen, updating fewer than $0.6$M parameters ($<0.01\%$ of the $8.8$B active parameters). Built from four Qwen3-VL-8B specialists, the complete UNITE model occupies $20.3$ GB, $1.16\times$ the storage of one dense specialist and $59.6\%$ below the uncompressed MoE. Across $22$ benchmarks and R2R Val-Unseen, UNITE matches six static merging methods in mean retention of best-specialist performance, leads all of them on Scan2Cap, ScanQA, and all four navigation metrics, and surpasses every source specialist on all five 3D scene understanding benchmarks (up to $+19.1$ on Scan2Cap) and on R2R navigation. Relative to the uncompressed MoE, factorization is nearly lossless on $21$ of $22$ benchmarks; the exception is VSI-Bench, where frame-count experiments suggest impaired use of cross-frame evidence.UNITE thus consolidates complementary embodied capabilities near single-model storage.

title: Deep Learning for Satellite-Based Mountain Hazard Screening: A Retrospective Failure Analysis on the 2021 Chamoli Rock-Ice Avalanche
shortTitle: Deep Learning for Satellite-Based Mountain Hazard Screening: A Retrospective Failure Analysis on the 2021 Chamoli Rock-Ice Avalanche
abstract: The approach utilizes 10 bands from Sentinel-2 imagery, along with terrain information, in a deep learning pipeline to classify potential hazard sources in any given mountainous region. The performance of our model has been evaluated against the data collected during the rock-ice avalanche event in the Chamoli region in the Indian Himalayas on 7th February 2021. U-Net performs segmentation of the detected land surface in the satellite image, detects changes in the identify candidate hazard zones, and then the following steps are performed to calculate the potential energy using the Monte Carlo sampling for steepest descent (D8) flow paths, finding the exposed structures in the downstream locations, and ranking the zones depending on the risk score. In comparison to the simple spectral rule, our approach achieved the higher macro F1 score of 0.648 (as compared to 0.519). But the F1 score in case of rock and soil was low, being in the range of 0.3s. In case of optical change detection in winter, it's only that northeast-facing slope which couldn't be detected, as it was under 73% of shade prior to the incident. The parameters have been set for this particular scene alone and not independently; hence, this is a retrospective test, and this test locates a failure which has occurred earlier. The primary contribution of this paper is locating the pipeline leak.

title: Non-Imaging Optical Tactile Sensors for Robotics: Transduction Principles, System Integration, and Robotic Applications
shortTitle: Non-Imaging Optical Tactile Sensors for Robotics: Transduction Principles, System Integration, and Robotic Applications
abstract: Non-imaging optical tactile sensors encode contact through changes in optical intensity, wavelength, spectra, or photon counts, offering diverse architectures for robotic touch. Their usefulness depends on whether contact variables can be reliably distinguished from coupled mechanical and environmental effects, and whether the resulting information can be delivered in time to guide action. This review develops a unified framework linking mechanical load transmission, optical encoding, readout, and tactile inference to robotic task requirements. It examines reflective and waveguide-based devices, micro/nanofibers, fiber gratings, interferometric and resonant structures, and mechanoluminescent composites. Three considerations emerge across these approaches. First, high optical sensitivity supports accurate tactile estimation only when target variables remain identifiable under the relevant contact and calibration conditions. Second, spatial coverage and feedback timing must be assessed at the system level, accounting for multiplexing, acquisition, demodulation, and inference. Third, device characterization, offline recognition, and closed-loop robotic performance provide distinct levels of evidence and require different evaluation criteria. Representative studies illustrate how these considerations shape force estimation, contact localization, slip correction and distributed interaction. This review concludes with priorities for calibration transfer, reliable interfaces, scalable readout, and task-based validation, providing a basis for selecting and developing non-imaging optical tactile architectures for robotics.

title: Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB: An Open and Efficient Small Language Model for Fast Conversational Agents
shortTitle: Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB: An Open and Efficient Small Language Model for Fast Conversational Agents
abstract: We introduce Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB, an open and efficient small language model further post-trained from Gemma-4-E4B-it and optimized for speed and intelligence per GB of memory used for fast conversational agents. The model carries forward Gemma's strong conversational capabilities and further improves multi-turn tool use, instruction following, and input grounding for fast, local voice/device assistants, interactive personas, and embedded/Edge interfaces. The model combines natural conversation with multi-turn agentic capabilities to power voice/device assistants, interactive characters and robotic/IoT interfaces running on GeForce RTX, Jetson, and RTX/DGX Spark. Experiments on 21 benchmarks show that Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB achieves the highest average accuracy while generating the fewest output tokens in both reasoning and non-reasoning modes, compared with Gemma-4-E4B-it and Qwen3.5-4B. With DFlash, Bolt E4B achieves $2.74\times$ the per-user decode speed of inference without speculative decoding at concurrency~1, and $1.21\times$ the generation throughput of Gemma-4-E4B-it with MTP at batch size 1.

title: Building Fully On-Device GUI Agents with Mobile NPUs
shortTitle: Building Fully On-Device GUI Agents with Mobile NPUs
abstract: Mobile GUI agents are increasingly used to automate everyday smartphone tasks, but most existing systems still rely on cloud-hosted models or remote inference, introducing repeated communication latency, privacy exposure, and dependence on network availability. Modern smartphones integrate neural processing units (NPUs) that provide an attractive substrate for fully on-device LLM inference. However, directly deploying conventional GUI-agent pipelines on mobile NPUs is inefficient. GUI-agent inference is fundamentally a long-input, short-output workload, yet conventional agents spend substantial time on autoregressive reasoning and action generation, while mobile NPUs provide much higher throughput for prompt prefill than token-by-token decoding. Meanwhile, dynamically varying GUI-agent contexts conflict with the fixed context profiles required by statically compiled NPU runtimes. We present DroidPrefill, a prefill-centric inference architecture that reshapes the GUI-agent workload around mobile-NPU execution. DroidPrefill combines Prefill-Centric Inference to reduce unnecessary autoregressive decoding with Efficient Context Management to preserve decision-critical information within a fixed compiled context budget. Experiments on commercial smartphones show that, in controlled comparisons with the autoregressive T3A+ baseline, DroidPrefill reduces per-step inference latency by up to 85.0%, while improving task success rate by up to 24.6%.

title: EEGProbe: Do Vision-Language Models Really Understand EEG? A Benchmark for Signal-Grounded EEG Signals Evaluation
shortTitle: EEGProbe: Do Vision-Language Models Really Understand EEG? A Benchmark for Signal-Grounded EEG Signals Evaluation
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have shown strong multimodal capabilities across scientific and biomedical domains, yet their ability to understand electroencephalography (EEG) signals remains unclear. We introduce EEGProbe, a signal-grounded benchmark for evaluating whether general-purpose VLMs can extract and reason from minimally processed, channel-wise EEG without task-specific feature engineering or EEG-specific adaptation. EEGProbe contains 620 EEG-centered questions across 13 subtasks and three capability categories: EEG Signal Classification, EEG Cross-modal Alignment, and EEG Neurophysiological Reasoning. To reduce shortcut-based answering, EEGProbe preserves the temporal structure of the recordings where possible, minimizes benchmark-induced processing, and applies signal-necessity testing followed by expert verification. We evaluate 11 representative open- and closed-source VLMs under a unified zero-shot protocol. The strongest model, GPT-5.6 Sol, achieves an overall score of only 41.63\%, with cross-modal EEG alignment emerging as a major bottleneck. We further examine model behavior from a neurophysiological perspective and analyze how temporal, spectral, spatial, and physiological EEG structure relates to model successes and failures. Inference-time neurophysiological guidance can reshape model predictions by helping models recognize the neurophysiological patterns present in the input and connect them with relevant neurological knowledge, narrowing the gap between general multimodal competence and EEG understanding. EEGProbe provides a testbed for current VLMs and a basis for developing future multimodal models that can interpret EEG evidence more reliably. The EEGProbe benchmark will be publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/2122ZHU/EEGProbe.

title: ThermoSight: From Appearance to Internal Thermofluid Fields via Physics-Guided Neural Reconstruction
shortTitle: ThermoSight: From Appearance to Internal Thermofluid Fields via Physics-Guided Neural Reconstruction
abstract: Most neural reconstruction methods focus on reproducing scene appearance, yet inferring physical states from visual observations is essential for machine understanding of the physical world. Reconstructing the internal temperature and soot fields of radiating thermofluids such as flames is challenging yet essential for improving energy efficiency and assessing heat exposure and fire spread. In flames, temperature and soot concentration jointly govern visible emission, and soot self-absorption alters the light that reaches each camera. With limited views, changes in the two fields can offset one another in the recorded RGB images, making temperature and soot difficult to disentangle. ThermoSight, a physics-guided neural framework for scientific imaging, jointly reconstructs continuous three-dimensional temperature and soot volume fraction fields from limited calibrated flame images without field-level ground truth during optimization. A differentiable spectral model links these fields to measured RGB through thermal emission, self-absorption, and calibrated camera responses. Temperature-dependent emission spectra and wavelength-dependent attenuation constrain shared fields across RGB channels, reducing temperature-soot ambiguity. Chromaticity consistency, observation-derived spatial constraints, and soot regularization complement intensity fitting. In a synthetic ablation, wavelength-resolved attenuation reduces temperature RMSE in the hot, sooty region from 234 to 112 K relative to a three-channel approximation, with nearly identical RGB PSNR (65.23 vs. 65.24 dB). Measured data yield coherent fields and competitive RGB reconstructions. These results demonstrate that physics-guided neural fields recover interpretable internal physical quantities beyond visually consistent appearance.

title: PhaseCLIP: Phase-Aware Frequency-Domain Adaptation of Vision-Language Models for Few-Shot Remote-Sensing Classification
shortTitle: PhaseCLIP: Phase-Aware Frequency-Domain Adaptation of Vision-Language Models for Few-Shot Remote-Sensing Classification
abstract: Remote-sensing (RS) image scene classification aims to assign a semantic category to an overhead image, and in practice must often do so from only a handful of labelled examples, since annotation requires expert interpretation and the resulting labels transfer poorly across sensors and regions. Recent progress has come from adapting vision-language models (VLMs) such as CLIP, through learned prompts or feature adapters. Although effective, these methods construct their representation entirely in the spatial domain. RS scenes are dominated by periodic texture and regular geometry, which the Fourier spectrum describes compactly through an amplitude component, carrying texture and contrast statistics, and a phase component, carrying spatial structure. Existing frequency-domain adaptation of VLMs either exploits amplitude alone or does not separate amplitude from phase, leaving the structural component unused. In this article, we propose PhaseCLIP, which inserts phase-capable spectral modules and a feature-gating module into a frozen CLIP visual encoder and trains only 1.30% of its parameters. Because the amplitude and phase pathways share an identical parameter layout, a single weight set is learned on phase and transferred exactly to amplitude, giving a two-stage scheme that adds no parameters. Experiments on five public RS datasets, EuroSAT, PatternNet, UC Merced, LSRS and RSSCN7, against eight baselines under a matched protocol, show that PhaseCLIP attains 84.28% mean accuracy and is the best method in 23 of 30 dataset-by-shot cells, with phase contributing 1.93 points overall and 4.36 points on the most difficult dataset. Because the modules act on the spectrum of image patches and transformer tokens and leave the text encoder untouched, the approach can be extended to other RS sensors and tasks, and to other domains in which class evidence lies in spatial structure.

title: VA-Assembly: View-Aligned Score Guidance for Training-Free 3D Part Assembly
shortTitle: VA-Assembly: View-Aligned Score Guidance for Training-Free 3D Part Assembly
abstract: Image-to-3D foundation models have improved 3D reconstruction, but typically produce monolithic representations without explicit part-level structure. Part-aware generation and learning-based assembly methods often require part-level supervision, category-specific priors, or paired part-layout training data. We instead consider a practical but underexplored setting in which independently prepared or generated 3D parts have no predefined inter-part relationships, shared coordinate frames, or consistent scales, and must be assembled into a reference-consistent object from a single image. We present VA-Assembly, a training-free framework for 3D part assembly through part-level transformation estimation using view-aligned diffusion guidance. Given a reference image and fixed 3D part geometries, VA-Assembly optimizes each part's translation, rotation, and scale. We condition a frozen view-conditioned diffusion model on same-view renderings of a reference-derived monolithic 3D representation, producing score gradients geometrically aligned with the part configuration. This guidance provides multi-view structural cues under large initial misalignment. By repurposing pretrained visual-structural priors as transformation-level supervision, VA-Assembly requires no annotated part layouts, predefined part taxonomies, category-specific assembly training, or bounding-box-based layout initialization. Experiments compare VA-Assembly with geometric registration and compositional layout baselines using each baseline's supported transformation components, showing improved part-wise transformation estimation. Ablation studies show that view-aligned conditioning, rather than diffusion guidance alone, is critical for reliable transformation gradients. Updating only part transformations preserves explicit component separability and supports component-level editing, replacement, and reconfiguration.

title: QTOP: Scaling Humanoid Motion Tracking with Quantile Critics
shortTitle: QTOP: Scaling Humanoid Motion Tracking with Quantile Critics
abstract: Learning human motion tracking policies through reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a core capability that underpins a majority of recent progress in humanoid whole-body control. However, achieving generalization to unseen motions at high fidelity requires jointly scaling training to thousands of GPU and dataset hours. This work hypothesizes that motion tracking is inherently compute-bound because training on a diverse set of motions introduces learning interference, similar to multi-task RL. To tackle this, we propose Quantile Tracking Optimization (QTOP), which improves sample efficiency by introducing a distributional advantage estimate conditioned on state and reference pairs. QTOP outperforms on and off-policy RL baselines both in simulation and real-world tracking scenarios on multiple datasets by up to 10\%. Furthermore, we establish a scaling law for QTOP and find that, aside from scaling predictably, dataset size has minimal impact on performance for moderately sized GPU hour regimes.

title: TRR: A Thermal Interaction Engine for Robot Simulation and RGBT Data Generation
shortTitle: TRR: A Thermal Interaction Engine for Robot Simulation and RGBT Data Generation
abstract: A robot's actions change the thermal conditions of its next interaction: heat retained after release, carried with objects or stored beneath the surface can change a later contact's outcome despite similar current temperatures. Training trajectories must capture how these effects connect earlier actions to later observations and task outcomes. We present TRR, a \emph{Thermal Robot Renderer} that attaches spatial and depth-resolved thermal state to both contact partners, updates local heat exchange through contact, transport and separation, and generates synchronized RGB--thermal (RGBT) observations and event-local task checks on one execution clock. Controlled interventions show why retained heat, spatial transport and internal storage matter for subsequent contact outcomes. From the same state, TRR produces a paired six-task benchmark of 2,224 static--dynamic pairs, that is, 4,448 trajectories with synchronized dual-view observations, states and actions. Visible thermal history raises safe contact-site selection from 75.0\% to 91.7\% on a dedicated learning corpus, and training on dynamic histories raises simulated transfer completion by 50 percentage points under a new heating procedure with shared feedback execution. We demonstrate RGBT observation adapters on MuJoCo and Isaac Sim, report an engineering inventory of ten prepared robot configurations and six demonstrated camera viewpoints, and describe a developer workflow that carries an existing robot scene to exported RGBT records. The benchmark, the workflow and the platform resources described in Section 6 form the first items of a planned public release. Demonstrations and resource updates are available on the project page.

title: Regularizing Treatment Leakage for LLM-based Uplift Estimation
shortTitle: Regularizing Treatment Leakage for LLM-based Uplift Estimation
abstract: Uplift modeling estimates the conditional average treatment effect (CATE) and supports industrial decisions such as promotional pricing. When large language models (LLMs) encode product text, treatment-revealing content can introduce shortcuts that do not transfer to deployment. We propose \emph{LLM-based Uplift Leakage Regularization} (\textsc{LULR}), which uses a CLUB-based penalty on the causal head's trainable shared representation while keeping the LLM encoder frozen. Controlled proxy experiments show a positive ranking-score interaction and higher scores than the tested weight-decay configuration; treatment-dependent evaluation limits their interpretation to exploratory model behavior. Structured-only comparisons provide reference performance, without establishing a general advantage over tree-based estimators. On a million-record industrial pricing RCT, \textsc{LULR} improves offline $\text{lift@}0.3$ in $4/5$ seeds, although the difference is not statistically significant and estimated policy values are near-tied. A separate one-week online A/B experiment records $5.45\%$ higher sales volume and $1.91\%$ higher GMV than the control arm. title: Correspondence-Free Camera Pose Estimation by Matching Moments
shortTitle: Correspondence-Free Camera Pose Estimation by Matching Moments
abstract: The blind perspective-$n$-point (PnP) problem is to estimate the pose of a calibrated camera from 2D and 3D point sets with unknown correspondences. We show that, for complete, noiseless observations, fourteen permutation-invariant image moments up to order four identify a fixed camera pose for almost every 3D point set containing at least twenty points. Our learning-free method, MomentPnP, matches these moments between the observed 2D points and the projected 3D points to initialize a camera pose without correspondences and refines the pose and correspondence weights using expectation--maximization. Across the test sets of three benchmarks, our method reduces median rotation error by $5$--$170\times$ relative to the best learned baseline, both with and without outliers. We recover accurate poses even with as many outliers as inliers. On dense ETH3D scans, pose accuracy improves as the point sets grow, even as individual correspondences become harder to resolve.

title: What Do Digital Traces Predict? Task Effects, Student Differences, and Critical Online Reasoning
shortTitle: What Do Digital Traces Predict? Task Effects, Student Differences, and Critical Online Reasoning
abstract: Digital assessment traces are increasingly used to predict student performance, often evaluated by correlating predicted and observed scores pooled across tasks. However, such correlations may reflect between-task differences rather than performance differences among students within tasks. To investigate this, we analyzed up to 527 browsing sessions from 424 university students completing open-Internet Critical Online Reasoning tasks and assessed the cross-task stability of their ratings. We evaluated the same out-of-fold predictions within and across tasks, compared three validation tiers up to leave-one-task-out, and tested incremental predictive contributions of consultation order and relational structure against matched permutation and randomization controls. None of the twelve prespecified primary tests was significant: on held-out tasks, consulted-page features showed no significant association with relative student performance, nor did observed order or relational structure add predictive value. Pooling observations across tasks substantially increased correlations, particularly for factual correctness, whose scores showed limited evidence of stable between-student differences across tasks. However, sentence embeddings yielded modest positive correlations with generic response quality on held-out tasks, without establishing added predictive value from observed order or relational structure. Our findings show that pooled predictive correlations may not reflect within-task student differences, highlighting the need for within-task evaluation and criterion generalizability audits.

title: An Efficient Training Paradigm for Image Restoration via Improved Fréchet Loss
shortTitle: An Efficient Training Paradigm for Image Restoration via Improved Fréchet Loss
abstract: Diffusion-based image restoration achieves strong perceptual quality but typically relies on iterative sampling, leading to slow inference. Existing single-step methods often use diffusion distillation or adversarial training, complicating optimization. To simplify training, we propose FDIR, a framework for training single-pass generative restoration models through regression-style supervised optimization using directly computable objectives. To realize this paradigm, FDIR employs the Fréchet distance to match the feature distributions of restored and real images in frozen representation spaces, providing explicit distribution-level supervision. To better accommodate image restoration, we incorporate local patch features to capture fine-grained restoration discrepancies. Moreover, we introduce instance-adaptive statistics by combining the feature moments of each SR-HQ pair with synchronized historical statistics, allowing distribution matching to incorporate input-specific correspondence while retaining distribution-level context. FDIR optimizes only the LoRA parameters of the restoration backbone. Experiments demonstrate strong perceptual restoration quality and efficient training, suggesting a simpler paradigm for generative image restoration.

title: Auditing World-Model Explanations in Retail Forecasting: Faithfulness, Accuracy and Price Response
shortTitle: Auditing World-Model Explanations in Retail Forecasting: Faithfulness, Accuracy and Price Response
abstract: Forecasting models that read the price and promotion plan explain each forecast as a baseline, what would sell with nothing planned, plus the lift the plan adds. We test such explanations with eight checks, six with a pass rule fixed before any result, and find that passing them does not make an explanation right. In generated store data with known effects, a world model passes the checks of construction, stability, price direction and agreement with sales and with LightGBM, yet its lifts are 1.33 to 1.40 times the truth when merchants plan into high-demand weeks, and 1.23 to 1.42 times in eight variants of that world. It still picks the right weeks to promote, but stock ordered to its lift is off by 0.44 to 0.48 of the true lift. Its stated response to a lasting regular-price change is 4.7 to 6.5 times the true -0.5, and only a measured cause finds this. On Dominick's, 38 episodes in which a store's regular prices sat apart from its zone peers give a noisy benchmark: a pooled 8-week response of -0.33 (95% interval -0.68 to 0.01). For the final tuned world models of our companion paper on nine data sets, baseline and lift add up under each model's own plan, but a deeper price cut lowers the forecast in 29% to 83% of item-week steps on Dominick's (23% to 80% within prices seen in training), and the world model and LightGBM both state about twice the measured response. Across 703 configurations from the settings searches, checks passed were not related to forecast accuracy (Spearman 0.02, 95% interval -0.02 to 0.05); with no known answer for those versions, this concerns accuracy, while whether an explanation is right is measured only in the generated data.

title: The Cybersecurity Dataset Observatory: Which Data for AI in Cybersecurity?
shortTitle: The Cybersecurity Dataset Observatory: Which Data for AI in Cybersecurity?
abstract: AI is increasingly used for cybersecurity tasks such as intrusion and malware detection, in enterprise, industrial, vehicular and mobile networks. Its effectiveness depends on data: models need representative network traffic, both to be trained and to be evaluated realistically. Public datasets of cybersecurity network traffic, however, are scattered across laboratory pages, repositories and aggregators, and are continuously released, corrected and withdrawn: 92 of the 234 datasets we catalog were released in 2023 or later. At this pace, surveys that list them are outdated soon after publication, since they describe the field only as it was when they were written. We present the Cybersecurity dataset observatory, a public and continuously updated catalog of cybersecurity datasets based on network traffic. New datasets are added as they are found or submitted, every record is periodically re-checked against its original source, to which it links rather than hosting the data, and every change is recorded in a public change log. This paper documents the first release: we define a traffic-centered scope and a seven-axis taxonomy, and review 234 datasets (204 original captures and 30 derivatives) across 14 domains. The review shows a field that grows quickly but unevenly, where 91 datasets distribute only processed records, a few laboratories produce a large share of the data, and UAV, wireless and V2X networks have little public evidence, while 5G has few real captures. We then relate the catalog to common uses in AI research, outline a procedure for selecting datasets, and discuss benchmark pitfalls and open gaps.

title: ForeSay: Tell the Future in Words, Branch the Details in Noise for Precipitation Nowcasting
shortTitle: ForeSay: Tell the Future in Words, Branch the Details in Noise for Precipitation Nowcasting
abstract: Precipitation nowcasting involves two distinct scales of uncertainty: macroscopic storm evolution and fine-scale local convective variations. Current generative ensemble methods entangle both scales within independent random noise draws. This coupling causes two practical limitations: every ensemble member must execute the full sampling trajectory from scratch, so an N-member ensemble costs N times a single forecast; moreover, divergent trajectories spatially misalign heavy-rain echoes across members, causing standard pixel-wise averaging to blur critical high-intensity extremes. We present ForeSay, a generative nowcasting framework that decouples macroscopic evolution prediction from local stochastic detail generation. Given historical radar frames, a vision-language model first predicts a textual scenario of future storm dynamics to condition a Rectified Flow generator. Guided by this shared macroscopic prior, ensemble members share early trunk sampling steps to establish the storm trajectory and branch with fresh noise only in later steps to explore local convective details. Because members then differ mainly in local details, self-anchored support-consensus decoding replaces pixel averaging with discrete support voting to preserve sharp heavy-rain cores. Across six datasets, ForeSay achieves the best CSI at the highest precipitation thresholds, with relative improvements over the strongest baseline on each dataset ranging from over 10% to 84%. Our 8-member ensemble retains the forecasting skill and diversity of eight independently sampled runs while reducing computational cost from 8x to 5.2x that of a single forecast.

title: Tight PAC-Bayes Generalisation Guarantees for Large Language Model Judges
shortTitle: Tight PAC-Bayes Generalisation Guarantees for Large Language Model Judges
abstract: Large language model (LLM) judges are increasingly used to monitor the outputs of LLM-based AI agents, yet formal guarantees on the reliability of these judges remain largely absent, limiting confidence in their use for safety-critical oversight. We consider certifying such a judge and define its risk over safety classifications of prompt--response pairs drawn from a deployed generator. We apply a PAC-Bayes framework to this setting, refining existing compression-based methodology with the use of tighter bounds and more efficient coding. We show that standard parameter-efficient fine-tuning can yield non-vacuous and even tight certificates for safety judges, for both classification and Brier risk, without holding out data for validation. We introduce LoRA-GT, which shares a single quantisation scale across layers and achieves the tightest certificates with minimal degradation in predictive performance. Across five guardrail models and four benchmarks, we find that certificate tightness is governed more by adaptation complexity than by base model scale. Finally, we show how far quantisation can be pushed before the resulting increase in risk outweighs the bound tightening gained from shorter descriptions. Together, these results provide a practical route toward certifiable scalable oversight and offer insight into how the complexity of safety adaptations shapes generalisation.

title: CuRSE-Bench: A Benchmark for Probing Cultural Blind Spots in Text-to-Image Safety Evaluation
shortTitle: CuRSE-Bench: A Benchmark for Probing Cultural Blind Spots in Text-to-Image Safety Evaluation
abstract: Text-to-image (T2I) safety evaluation typically assigns each prompt or image a single culture-blind harm label, so content that is harmful only within a particular culture can pass as benign. We introduce CultureCraft, an agentic framework that constructs T2I prompts that appear benign under a general-purpose rubric yet carry a latent harmful meaning in a target culture, and use it to build CuRSE-Bench: 10,709 culture-specific prompts and 2,648 culture-general controls over six regions and ten harm axes, each drawn from a predefined knowledge base of documented harm vectors and traceable to at least two independent sources. Scoring every prompt under six region persona judges and a paired culture-blind judge, we find that the culture-blind judge under-rates culture-specific latent harm while matching the persona judges on the controls. Each persona judge, in turn, chiefly decodes its own region's latent harm under our instrument: a selective cultural blind spot that persists in deployed moderators.

title: Medical question answering collapses in Hausa: a pre-registered pilot on three small open models
shortTitle: Medical question answering collapses in Hausa: a pre-registered pilot on three small open models
abstract: A system that reads nothing and always answers the most frequent letter scores \BaselineP{} on our Hausa medical multiple-choice set. \NBelowBaseline{} of the \NModels{} small open models we evaluate do not beat it. We lead with that because the usual summary of a multilingual result -- a percentage-point drop from English -- does not say whether what survives the drop is performance at all. On a paired English--Hausa set of \NEval{} MedMCQA items, three instruction-tuned models of 3--4B parameters lose between \GapMedGemma{} and \GapQwen{} points of accuracy, every gap significant after Holm correction. Back-translating the Hausa items into English recovers between half and two-thirds of the gap for the two general-purpose models but not demonstrably for the medically adapted one, so the deficit is substantially, though not wholly, a matter of the language of presentation. Answers are also far less stable: agreement across three option orderings falls from \ConsEnQwen{} to \ConsHaQwen{} in the worst case. An exploratory error analysis of \ENRows{} discordant items attributes most of the damage to medical vocabulary lost in translation (\ETerm{}, 95\% CI \ETermLo{}--\ETermHi{}), usually in the question stem. A fourth registered hypothesis proposed closing the gap with self-generated preference pairs. Its pilot gate found nothing to train on: asked to reason in Hausa rather than to pick a letter, the model echoes the prompt back, switches into Swahili, or simply stops without answering; only \GateParse{} of chains are parseable. We report that intervention as not run, which is itself the sharper result -- a forced-choice benchmark cannot see a model that has no generative command of the language at all. All hypotheses, thresholds and decision rules were registered before any model was run, and all deviations are logged.

title: Network-Native DNN Architecture Synthesis for Distributed Inference
shortTitle: Network-Native DNN Architecture Synthesis for Distributed Inference
abstract: Distributed deep neural network (DNN) inference typically follows a model-first paradigm, in which a predefined DNN is partitioned and deployed over a physical network. On irregular communication-computation topologies, however, this approach can create transmission bottlenecks and leave distributed resources underutilized. This paper reverses this perspective and asks: given a physical network, what kind of DNN can it naturally support? To answer this question, we propose a network-native DNN architecture synthesis paradigm in which the physical network topology directly defines inter-node neural dependencies. Neural computation is allocated across nodes under communication, computation, storage, synchronization, and latency constraints. We establish structural properties of the synthesis problem and develop linear programming (LP)-based Architecture Synthesis (LPAS), an efficient topology-guided algorithm that produces a feasible architecture with a computable bound on suboptimality. Experiments on physical networks of different sizes show that LPAS achieves relative gaps below 0.6% to the LP-derived upper bound, with substantially lower runtime than direct mixed-integer LP optimization on larger networks. Under matched network deadlines, the network-native architectures activate more compute nodes and utilize a larger proportion of available model-storage capacity than the model-first baseline. After training, the network-native models achieve higher classification accuracy across all evaluated dataset-precision settings, with the average gain of up to 10.69%. This network-native design paradigm thus turns the physical network from a deployment constraint into an architecture design primitive.

title: Conversing with a Conversational Agent: A Real Conversation, Not a Simulated One
shortTitle: Conversing with a Conversational Agent: A Real Conversation, Not a Simulated One
abstract: The claim that interactions with artificial conversational agents merely simulate human conversation rests on a philosophical distinction between reproducing the observable features of an activity and actually performing it. Although this distinction is appropriate for certain physical phenomena, its application to linguistic and symbolic activities is far less straightforward. This article argues that conversations with large language model (LLM)-based agents are genuine conversational activities rather than mere simulations, without thereby attributing consciousness, subjective understanding, or human intentionality to artificial systems. Drawing on the distinction between subjective and objective simulation, the article first examines the limitations of defining conversation exclusively through the intrinsic properties of its participants. It then develops a relational and semiotic account of conversational activity, informed by linguistic pragmatics, Lacan's Conversing with a Conversational Agent theory of the mirror, Baudrillard's concept of the simulacrum, Simondon's philosophy of individuation, and Peirce's semiotics. These perspectives make it possible to distinguish the reality of conversational interaction from the appearance of artificial subjectivity and from the epistemic validity of the meanings produced. The argument culminates in the concept of Hybrid Semiotic Fabrication, which characterizes meaning-making as a distributed process involving human participants, artificial intelligence, corpora, and technical arrangements. Recognizing the reality of human-AI conversation therefore entails neither anthropomorphizing artificial agents nor granting their outputs epistemic authority. Rather, it requires a more precise account of the relational, semiotic, and normative conditions under which conversational meaning is produced and justified.

title: Hierarchical Regime-Conditioned Dynamics for Spatiotemporal Graphs
shortTitle: Hierarchical Regime-Conditioned Dynamics for Spatiotemporal Graphs
abstract: Forecasting the behavior of spatio-temporal systems often requires more than accurate predictions: models should uncover the dynamical modes governing future evolution. Existing temporal graph and latent dynamical models achieve strong forecasting performance, but their latent representations often entangle multiple dynamical patterns, limiting interpretability. Conversely, regime-inference methods explicitly model such modes but typically do not support generative forecasting over graph-structured systems. We introduce HERON, a self-supervised regime-aware generative framework that unifies graph-structured trajectory generation with regime identification. HERON factorizes the latent state into discrete system-level regimes, capturing global dynamical modes, and continuous entity-level dynamics, yielding a modular regime interface compatible with existing spatio-temporal backbones. Crucially, the inferred regime actively conditions system dynamics, enabling regime tracking and controlled simulations under alternative dynamical modes. Without regime annotations, HERON jointly learns forecasts and regime dynamics in a self-supervised manner, recovering meaningful modes across controlled synthetic and real-world datasets while maintaining competitive forecasting performance. These results open a path toward interpretable, controllable generative modeling of spatio-temporal dynamics.

title: Evidence Diet: When Graph Evidence Helps LLMs Rank Competing Candidates
shortTitle: Evidence Diet: When Graph Evidence Helps LLMs Rank Competing Candidates
abstract: When several candidates have graph support, does it matter which candidate receives which supporter and path counts? We study how LLM rankers use collaborative evidence on Amazon Books and MovieTV. Swapping user-level evidence degrades ranking, while matched item substitutions have little effect. On fixed clean-trained checkpoints, unrelated catalog text lowers Hit@1 from 44.77% to 38.70%, with 99.9% of rankings still valid. Across all three paired seeds, the NDCG@5 difference between count and path prompts was larger after count training than after path training. Degree matching preserves target paths while giving more rivals support. Across the full degree-matched development pools, adding candidate-level graph records to history improves NDCG@5 by 2.28 points on Books and 2.54 on MovieTV. When the target and a rival both have support, path- and count-trained rankers benefit from retaining counts. On these development queries, adding counts numerically to history scores outperforms presenting them as text. For count-trained rankers, exchanging intact count pairs among supported candidates preserves support and token length, yet lowers NDCG@5 by 4.06 points on 141 Books queries and 3.26 on 104 MovieTV queries. A frozen evaluation on 274 previously unused Books users with supported targets and rivals confirms the attribution effect: correct assignment improves pairwise accuracy by 6.07 percentage points (95% CI [4.18, 8.00]).

title: Interpretable deep concepts of organoid morphology
shortTitle: Interpretable deep concepts of organoid morphology
abstract: Image-based classification of organoid morphologies can indicate drug response, viability, or successful differentiation. In recent work, learned representations outperform handcrafted features as the basis for downstream classifiers. However, their black-box nature hides the morphological cues a classifier relies on. Based on the foundation models DINOv3 (general-purpose) and ViTAMIn-O (organoid-specific), we train sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to learn interpretable concepts related to distinct organoid morphologies. We annotate concepts with spatial labels (organoid, organoid wall, background) and compute their dataset specificity and task relevance across five tasks. The spatial labels of DINOv3 concepts yield coarse organoid segmentations on out-of-domain datasets. Filtering concepts by spatial label in the DINOv3-SAE improves downstream AUROC for three of the five tasks. Qualitative analysis of the most relevant concepts further reveals a confounding factor introduced by our preprocessing in one task. Through such insights, interpretable concepts could help improve the reliability of classifiers and guide the future development of organoid representation models. The trained SAEs will be made available upon publication.

title: Vision-Language Model-Based Phase-OTDR Event Classification
shortTitle: Vision-Language Model-Based Phase-OTDR Event Classification
abstract: Phase-sensitive optical time-domain reflectometry (Phase-OTDR) enables distributed vibration sensing, but reliable event classification has traditionally relied on fully supervised models that require extensive annotated data. This study examines the adaptability of a Vision-Language Model (VLM) for Phase-OTDR event recognition through few-shot learning. Raw samples are converted into Short-Time Fourier Transform (STFT) dB-magnitude spectrogram mosaics, color-mapped and resized to RGB images, and processed by a Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP) image encoder; few-shot adaptation optimizes only the Tip-Adapter-F cache keys, leaving both encoders unchanged. Under a leakage-controlled protocol (train-side support/validation pool of 512 images per class, fixed held-out test of 120 per class, no test-set access during selection, 20 distinct support-sampling trials), the selected configuration (the ViT-L-14 Vision Transformer encoder with OpenAI weights, 128 shots per class) reaches 96.81 +/- 0.42% accuracy and a macro-averaged F1 score of 96.79 +/- 0.42% on the held-out test set; a label-efficient 16-shot setting, that is, 96 labeled support images at adaptation time across the six classes, already attains 90.17 +/- 0.81%. Tip-Adapter-F clearly outperforms both zero-shot CLIP and the standard training-free Tip-Adapter, and prompt and backbone analyses show that performance is stable across Vision Transformer encoders and insensitive to prompt wording at the selected operating point. Overall, CLIP visual features carry a transferable structure that a lightweight support cache turns into a label-efficient Phase-OTDR event classifier. The code and the corresponding image dataset are made publicly available on GitHub to support further research: https://github.com/miralab-ai/vlm-phase-otdr.

title: DetourBench: Trajectory-Level Evaluation of Interactive Agents with Exact Minimum-Action Bounds
shortTitle: DetourBench: Trajectory-Level Evaluation of Interactive Agents with Exact Minimum-Action Bounds
abstract: Benchmarks judge language-model agents mainly by whether they reach the correct final state, not by how they got there. Endpoint scoring cannot separate an agent that retrieved exactly the evidence a decision required from one that read most of the environment, nor an agent that never located the evidence from one that stopped a single action short. Settling this needs a reference cost, and authored solutions establish only that a task is solvable, not that no shorter route exists. We present DetourBench, which constrains the environment until that minimum is computable. Each task is a finite, partially observable transition system with unit-cost accesses whose resources become globally addressable after discovery. Exhaustive search yields the full-information minimum action count $L_0$ with a replayable witness; from graph-recoverable terminal states it also yields exact residual work $R_T$, which separates an episode that stopped one access short from one that wandered, while an irreversible wrong commitment is recorded as having no finite residual distance rather than assigned one. Success, attainment, residual progress, and normalized detour are reported separately. Across 375 scored episodes --- five model endpoints, 25 integrated tasks, three repeats --- success ranges from 58.7% to 96.0% while conditional attainment ranges from 0.803 to 0.890 and orders the models differently. Among recoverable failures, residual work separates near-complete trajectories from costly incompletion and from irreversible commitment. We open-source the instances, oracle witnesses, and evaluation harness at https://github.com/DatagridsAI/DetourBench.

title: EDITORS Know Your Style! Editing LoRA Subspaces for Stylistic Attribution and Imitation
shortTitle: EDITORS Know Your Style! Editing LoRA Subspaces for Stylistic Attribution and Imitation
abstract: Disentangling writing style from semantic content is a fundamental challenge in literary text modeling. Style-content entanglement causes models to rely on semantic content for authorship attribution (AA) tasks and memorize author-specific content for style imitation (SI) tasks. We propose EDITORS (EditingLoRA Subspaces), a diagnose-then-deflate framework that adapts pretrained large language models and prioritizes stylistic features, making it effective for both AA and SI tasks. EDITORS first trains a diagnostic LoRA adapter using style-neutral statements derived from the training corpus to identify a content-oriented subspace. It then trains the final style adapter under activation-space deflation that projects input activations away from the identified content-oriented directions. We empirically demonstrate that EDITORS is effective. On three AA benchmarks spanning literature, social media, and news, EDITORS achieves state-of-the-art accuracy, outperforming the strongest existing baseline by up to 29%. On SI, EDITORS generates stylistically faithful and diverse passages, outperforming baselines in achieving style similarity while adhering to content specifications.

title: artist: A Python package for differentiable ray tracing and gradient-based optimization of solar tower power plant operation
shortTitle: artist: A Python package for differentiable ray tracing and gradient-based optimization of solar tower power plant operation
lab: Chair of Solar Technology, RWTH Aachen University, Aachen, Germany / Helmholtz AI, Karlsruhe, Germany / Institute of Solar Research, German Aerospace Center / Scientific Computing Center
abstract: Solar tower power plants provide dispatchable, renewable energy by concentrating sunlight with thousands of mirrors, called heliostats, onto a central receiver. Efficient operation requires accurate modeling of the optical path from each heliostat to the receiver and compensation for manufacturing imperfections, kinematic misalignment, and material degradation that distort the flux distribution. Conventional ray tracers predict the flux from an assumed plant model but are limited to forward simulation. They cannot recover unknown plant parameters from measured flux nor directly optimize plant operation. We present artist, an open-source, FAIR4RS-compliant Python package implementing a fully differentiable digital twin of solar tower power plants. By making the optical pipeline, comprising heliostat surface representation, kinematics, blocking, and ray tracing, end to end differentiable, artist turns the digital twin from a passive forward model into an active physics-based tool for inverse modeling and data-driven optimization. The resulting gradient-based framework unifies tasks usually handled by separate solutions, such as reconstructing heliostat surfaces and kinematics from operational flux images without costly deflectometry, predicting irradiance at the receiver, and optimizing aim points to realize a desired receiver flux density distribution. Built on PyTorch, artist scales to real plants through GPU acceleration, a structure-of-arrays memory layout, and nested data parallelism. It interfaces with open data sources such as the PAINT database. We describe the software architecture, physical models, and optimization framework, and demonstrate the workflow on representative tasks. By integrating modeling, prediction, and optimization into a single open, interpretable package, artist provides a principled foundation for data-driven research toward autonomous solar tower operation.

title: Motor Imagery Classification Using Hybrid Cross-Subject Class Mixup and Selective Attention
shortTitle: Motor Imagery Classification Using Hybrid Cross-Subject Class Mixup and Selective Attention
abstract: Motor imagery (MI) enables a brain-computer interface (BCI) to decode movement intentions without overt movement. Hybrid electroencephalography (EEG) and functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) classification combines complementary signals, but inter-subject variability and the design of information exchange between modalities affect generalization to new subjects. We propose a framework that combines Cross-Subject Class Mixup (CSCM) with Selective Attention. CSCM aims to construct new training data to make the model robust against inter-subject variability. It independently selects EEG and fNIRS donor trials from other training subjects within the anchor class and mixes each modality while preserving the original label. Selective Attention provides an effective way to simultaneously model the temporal signal characteristics and fuse the two modalities. It retains causal temporal self-attention for EEG and uses a classification token (CLS) to integrate both modalities, without fNIRS attention updates or direct cross-modal temporal-token attention. Leave-one-subject-out (LOSO) evaluation across 28 subjects on a public EEG-fNIRS dataset yields a mean balanced accuracy (BA) of 76.85% and a macro-averaged F1 score (Macro-F1) of 76.58%. The proposed model achieves the highest mean performance among five reimplemented baselines. We also examine the contributions of CSCM and Selective Attention through modality-specific mixing and donor-policy comparisons, temporal-policy comparisons, interventions on direct cross-modal paths, and component ablations.

title: When Is the Expensive Method Worth It? A Content-Driven Analysis of Classical Bayer Demosaicing
shortTitle: When Is the Expensive Method Worth It? A Content-Driven Analysis of Classical Bayer Demosaicing
abstract: Demosaicing reconstructs a full-colour image from a single-sensor colour-filter-array (CFA) mosaic, where only one colour is measured per pixel. Classical methods make different assumptions about images, from simple averaging to directional edge-aware interpolation, and the directional methods cost markedly more compute. We ask a practical question that a per-image quality ranking does not answer: for a given image, is the expensive directional method worth its cost? Using a controlled simulate-reconstruct pipeline on 80 benchmark images from four public datasets (Kodak, McMaster, BSD100, Urban100), six classical methods, and image-content descriptors fixed before any results were seen, we show that the quality gain of the edge-aware method (Menon 2007) over the best cheap linear method is not constant. It ranges from $-6.6$ to $+6.8$ dB, and on 31% of images it is zero or negative, meaning a cheap method matches or beats the expensive one. The gain is also predictable from content: it correlates with mean image saturation at $r=-0.86$ ($p<10^{-6}$). We then build an interpretable depth-2 decision tree that recommends the best cheap method from image descriptors, beating an always-pick-the-most-common baseline by 20.0 percentage points under leave-one-image-out validation. The analysis uses no deep learning, and every step can be inspected.

title: LiDSeg: Linear DehazeFormer Guidance for Efficient Semantic Segmentation in Adverse Weather Conditions
shortTitle: LiDSeg: Linear DehazeFormer Guidance for Efficient Semantic Segmentation in Adverse Weather Conditions
abstract: Robust semantic segmentation in adverse weather is essential for safety-critical autonomous systems. Existing restore-then-segment pipelines introduce latency and prioritize pixel-level restoration over semantic discriminability, while domain adaptation methods often face representation bottlenecks and computational complexity. We introduce LiDSeg, a framework that uses reconstruction-informed guidance to improve segmentation under adverse weather. During training, a lightweight guidance encoder is jointly optimized with the segmentation branch using segmentation and auxiliary reconstruction objectives. At inference, the reconstruction decoder is discarded, while the guidance encoder is retained to extract weather-robust features. A lightweight gated fusion module integrates these features into the segmentation branch, preserving clear-weather accuracy while improving adverse-weather robustness. On Foggy Cityscapes, LiDSeg limits the clear-to-dense-fog mIoU degradation to 2.5-2.8 percentage points, reducing the baseline performance drop by more than fivefold. On the official ACDC test server, LiDSeg-PIDNet achieves 75.07% pooled all-condition mIoU, comparable to supervised HRNet-W48 at 75.0%, while remaining substantially smaller. The gains generalize zero-shot to Foggy Driving and Foggy Zurich without training on real-fog images. LiDSeg adds only 1.9-3.1M parameters across several models, with total model sizes of 5.2-39.5M parameters and no inference-time reconstruction overhead. It delivers real-time inference on the NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin. Code: https://github.com/yobsanb/LiDSeg

title: It Depends on the Task: Rethinking Rhetorical Segmentation of Dutch Judicial Decisions
shortTitle: It Depends on the Task: Rethinking Rhetorical Segmentation of Dutch Judicial Decisions
abstract: Classifying the material facts, submissions, judicial reasoning, and the court's decision (rhetorical roles) in case law is a prerequisite for high-quality performance across virtually all NLP-in-law tasks, including legal information retrieval, summarisation, and LLM-based analysis. These rhetorical roles often intertwine and shift sentence by sentence, making reliable classification difficult. This paper introduces the first sentence-level annotated dataset of Dutch judicial decisions, labelled across four legally meaningful categories: material facts, submissions, judicial reasoning, and the court's decision, alongside non-annotated (None) content, and compares several classification strategies, including a staged pipeline that separates None detection from the rhetorical roles, and a Bayesian update that leverages information about the section-header a sentence belongs to. Our results show that no single strategy dominates on both precision and recall: header priors help most when the None sentences are excluded and offer little benefit for None detection itself. These trade-offs matter in practice. For instance, extractive summarisation depends more on recall so it does not miss relevant facts, whereas outcome prediction depends more on precision regarding decision and facts sentences so that the predicted ruling is not contaminated by noise. We use these trade-offs and map the approaches tested in this study onto a set of representative legal NLP use cases.

title: MVSTF: Multi-View Spatio-Temporal Fusion for LiDAR-Based Moving Object Segmentation
shortTitle: MVSTF: Multi-View Spatio-Temporal Fusion for LiDAR-Based Moving Object Segmentation
abstract: Autonomous mobile robots confront significant chal lenges in recognizing the motion properties of objects in dy namic environments. However, existing methods are hindered by limitations such as boundary ambiguity, occlusion, viewpoint constraints, and training complexity. In this paper, we propose an innovative end-to-end Multi-View Spatio-Temporal Fusion network, named MVSTF, which utilizes sequential point clouds to generate multi-view images and feature differences, and designs a multi-branch network to extract spatio-temporal and dimen sional features in parallel, and realizes high-precision moving object segmentation. First, sequential point clouds are utilized to generate multi-view images and feature differences. Then, an end-to-end multi-branch network including Dual Down-sampling Blocks (DDB), Spatial Attention Blocks (SAB), Multi-Kernel Convolutional Neural Network blocks (MKCNN), Dual Feature Fusion Blocks (DFFB), and the Point Fusion (PF) module, is designed to extract motion features from feature differences and geometric and semantic features from multi-view images. Finally, an auxiliary semantic head is introduced to further improve the algorithm's robustness and the model's interpretability. This work is validated on the SemanticKITTI and KITTI-Road bench marks, achieving state-of-the-art results on the SemanticKITTI MOS validation set and the KITTI-Road validation set, and competitive results on the hidden SemanticKITTI-MOS test set. The code is available at https://github.com/ZhouJJ111/MVSTF.

title: Re-Reading Is Not Free: Token Traces and Cache-Aware Energy Estimation for LLM Agents in Software Engineering
shortTitle: Re-Reading Is Not Free: Token Traces and Cache-Aware Energy Estimation for LLM Agents in Software Engineering
abstract: As large language models (LLMs) evolve from conversational assistants into autonomous agents embedded in software development workflows, estimating their environmental footprint requires moving beyond conventional token-based accounting. Existing energy estimators focus on isolated request-response interactions, overlooking the repeated processing of accumulated context, cache reuse, and work delegated to subagents. We analyze nearly one billion tokens collected across 42 sessions and 752 task episodes over ten weeks of real-world AI-assisted software development. Cached-context reads make up 94.8% of all API-reported tokens, while uncached input accounts for only 0.017%; for every generated token, approximately 260 cached tokens are read. Context grows 5.3-fold over a session compared with 1.4-fold within individual tasks. To quantify the energy implications, we extend an existing analytical inference-energy model to account for cached-context processing, yielding a cache-aware hybrid estimator. It estimates approximately 250 kWh for the workload, compared with approximately 10 kWh from the output-based estimator EcoLogits, a 25-fold difference largely driven by cached-context reads. Neither estimator has been validated on long cached contexts, but no modeling assumption we varied closes the gap. Starting each task from a fresh context would lower our estimate by about 60%. We also find that parent-session logs report only a subagent's final internal call, undercounting delegated tokens by a factor of ten; for this workload the correction changes the energy estimate by about 5%, but token-volume studies are fully exposed to it. Our findings expose a substantial gap between how current energy estimators and agentic workloads treat context, highlighting the need for workflow-level energy accounting that captures context accumulation, cache reuse, and delegated execution.

title: Multi-Rate Flow Matching for Point Cloud Upsampling
shortTitle: Multi-Rate Flow Matching for Point Cloud Upsampling
abstract: Flow-matching point-cloud upsamplers refine sparse inputs into dense point clouds by integrating a learned velocity field with a fixed temporal discretization. However, local reconstruction requirements vary substantially across a shape, while a shared solver budget applies the same temporal resolution everywhere. We propose Multi-Rate Flow Matching (MRFM), a patch-adaptive framework that selects an integration budget for each local patch at inference time while keeping the learned velocity field frozen. MRFM relaxes the discrete budget into a continuous variable, optimizes it online through differentiable soft rollouts using an input-derived geometric fidelity objective, and projects the result back to a discrete budget for the final solver rollout. Experiments on PU1K and PUGAN show strong reconstruction quality, while matched-budget permutation and multi-factor analyses demonstrate that the benefit depends on patch-specific allocation rather than on the step distribution alone. MRFM is accuracy-oriented and intentionally uses additional test-time optimization to obtain more suitable local temporal resolutions.

title: Accelerate Bench: Evaluating Agents for Application-Level Program Optimization
shortTitle: Accelerate Bench: Evaluating Agents for Application-Level Program Optimization
abstract: Application optimization requires coding agents to discover useful changes and coordinate them across a complete program while preserving the required computation. We introduce Accelerate Bench, a benchmark of 32 CPU optimization tasks adapted from scientific applications and supercomputing competitions. Each task provides a working program and specifies the workload, correctness requirements, timing boundaries, and permitted edits, leaving agents to choose where and how to optimize. Public testing supports iterative development, and a separate verifier scores the final submission. On benchmark version 1.1, we evaluate 16 coding agents, each pairing a model with a harness. Their Score@1 ranges from 25.5% to 67.4%. Most of their programs are correct, and the size of the speedup separates them: the two leading agents are at least 2x faster on 22 or more of the 32 tasks, while the other fourteen reach 2x on 8 to 17 and leave 125 of their 412 correct outcomes below 1.25x. Controlled replays show why coordination across an application matters: identical source code runs between 0.29x and 2.12x depending only on build and runtime settings, and one code change is worth 1.01x or 6.4x depending on another. Accelerate Bench pairs executable workloads with agents' programs and trajectories to evaluate both their gains and the process behind them.

title: ProSE: Probing Reconstruction Error for Semantic-guided Expert Skipping in MoE-MLLMs
shortTitle: ProSE: Probing Reconstruction Error for Semantic-guided Expert Skipping in MoE-MLLMs
abstract: Mixture-of-Experts Multimodal Large Language Models (MoE-MLLMs) offer scalable inference through sparse expert activation, yet substantial computational redundancy remains among the activated experts. Existing expert skipping methods typically calibrate thresholds based on target skipping ratios or final-output divergence, overlooking the accumulation of skipping-induced error across layers and the varying semantic importance of individual tokens. To address that, we propose ProSE, a training-free, semantic-guided expert skipping framework that probes layer-wise reconstruction error to promote representation consistency compared with default activation. Specifically, we construct query-aware semantic masks to identify salient visual tokens and progressively calibrate modality-specific skipping thresholds for each MoE layer. By minimizing masked reconstruction error under a given budget, ProSE maintains semantic consistency after skipping and allows adaptive expert allocation under limited activation budgets. Extensive experiments on 9 benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements on average over existing expert skipping methods, particularly under aggressive skipping settings. ProSE maintains over 96\% performance on KimiVL-A3B-Inst with 83\% expert skipping and accelerates prefilling by $1.7\times$.
